title: Sleep deprivation increases levels of the synaptic density marker SV2A in the human brain
experiments_summary: Forty healthy volunteers (14 female, 26 male; mean age 27.5 years) were randomized to either a sleep deprivation group (n=20) or a control group (n=20). All participants underwent a one-week ambulatory sleep satiation protocol (9 hours time-in-bed confirmed by actigraphy) with caffeine abstinence, followed by an adaptation and baseline night with sleep EEG recording. Each participant received two [18F]SynVesT-1 PET scans: a baseline scan and a second scan either after 28 hours of total sleep deprivation (sleep deprivation group) or after a normal night of sleep (control group). PET scans were acquired on a 3 Tesla PET/MR system (BrainPET; Siemens Healthineers) with 90-minute scan durations. The radiotracer [18F]SynVesT-1 was synthesized using a GMP-compliant automated radiosynthesis process. PET data were reconstructed using OP-OSEM and preprocessed with the PMOD Neuro Tool pipeline, including motion correction, MRI co-registration, and spatial normalization to MNI space. Binding potential (BPND) was quantified using the Simplified Reference Tissue Model 2 (SRTM2) with an eroded centrum semiovale as the reference region and a fixed population-based k2' of 0.032. Eight bilateral brain regions of interest (frontal, cingulate, occipital, parietal, and temporal cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, and striatum) were defined using the AAL atlas intersected with individual gray matter segments. Sleep-deprived participants remained awake in the laboratory under continuous staff supervision and were given a 2-hour recovery sleep opportunity after the second PET scan, during which EEG was recorded using a wireless DREEM 3 headband. Slow wave activity (SWA; 0.5–4 Hz delta power) was computed from the first 1.5 hours after sleep onset during both baseline and recovery sleep using the YASA Python toolbox. Cognitive performance was measured before each PET scan using a 3-minute Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), and subjective sleepiness was assessed with the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS). Control participants wore an actigraph between visits to confirm absence of daytime napping. Statistical analyses were performed in SAS 9.4 using random-subject mixed ANOVAs on the scan-to-scan difference in SV2A BPND, with group, brain region, and their interaction as fixed factors and subject as a random factor. Post-hoc comparisons were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the false discovery rate. Pearson correlations were computed between individual changes in SV2A BPND and changes in SWA, PVT performance, and KSS scores. PVT and KSS differences between groups were compared using unpaired Wilcoxon tests.
